canonical_statement: The review summarizes patient-oriented evidence on the diagnosis and management of onychomycosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This article provides a summary of the best available patient-oriented evidence on the diagnosis and management of this condition.

canonical_statement: The authors searched PubMed Clinical Queries using the terms onychomycosis, tinea unguium, and nail fungus.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A PubMed search was completed in Clinical Queries using the key terms onychomycosis, tinea unguium, and nail fungus.

canonical_statement: The PubMed search included meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, and reviews.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The search included meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, and reviews.

canonical_statement: The authors also searched the Cochrane database, DynaMed, and Essential Evidence Plus; reported search dates were November 13, 2020 and August 15, 2021.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: database, DynaMed, and Essential Evidence Plus. Search dates: November 13, 2020, and August 15, 2021.

canonical_statement: The authors reported no relevant financial affiliations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Author disclosure: No relevant financial affiliations.

canonical_statement: The review reports an estimated adult point prevalence of onychomycosis in North America of up to 13.8%.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The estimated point prevalence of onychomycosis in North America is up to 13.8% for adults

canonical_statement: The review reports a point prevalence of onychomycosis of 0.44% in children and adolescents younger than 18 years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: and 0.44% for children and adolescents younger than 18 years.

population.label: Children and adolescents younger than 18 years

canonical_statement: The review identifies age older than 60 years as an important onychomycosis risk factor, attributed to poorer peripheral circulation, suboptimal immune function, slower nail growth, and longer fungal exposure.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Age older than 60 years is an important risk factor because of poor peripheral circulation, suboptimal immune function, slower nail growth

canonical_statement: Other reported risk factors include recurrent nail trauma, tobacco use, diabetes mellitus, obesity, psoriasis, malignancy, HIV, peripheral vascular disease, and immunocompromised states.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Other risk factors include recurrent nail trauma, tobacco use, and certain comorbidities

canonical_statement: The review reports that dermatophytes cause about 70% of U.S. onychomycosis infections and nondermatophyte molds and yeasts account for the remaining 30%.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dermatophytes cause 70% of onychomycosis infections in the United States, with the remaining 30% caused by nondermatophyte molds and yeasts.

population.label: Onychomycosis infections in the United States

quantitative_result.original_result_text: 70% dermatophytes; remaining 30% nondermatophyte molds and yeasts

canonical_statement: The review cites a study in which 39% of onychomycosis infections were mixed infections involving dermatophytes plus mold and/or yeast.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: One study showed that 39% of infections were mixed

population.label: Onychomycosis infections in the cited study

canonical_statement: The review states that fungi account for about 50% of nail dystrophies, so the differential diagnosis for abnormal nails is broad.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: With fungi causing 50% of nail dystrophies, the differential diagnosis for nail abnormalities is large

concept.text: Proportion of nail dystrophies due to fungi

canonical_statement: Common clinical features include discoloration, deformity, hypertrophy or hyperkeratosis, subungual debris, nail-bed separation, brittle or crumbling nails, and foul odor.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Common signs and symptoms of onychomycosis include nails that appear discolored, deformed, hypertrophic, or hyperkeratotic

canonical_statement: The Onychomycosis Severity Index grades disease using area involved, proximity to the nail matrix, and dermatophytoma or subungual hyperkeratosis greater than 2 mm.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: uses three clinical features to assess severity: area of involvement, proximity of disease to the nail matrix

canonical_statement: The review recommends laboratory confirmation of nail infection for accurate diagnosis before treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Laboratory confirmation of nail infection is important for accurate diagnosis.

canonical_statement: Potassium hydroxide preparation with direct microscopy is the preferred diagnostic method because it is highly specific, rapid, and cost-effective.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation with direct microscopy is the preferred diagnostic method

concept.text: Potassium hydroxide preparation with direct microscopy

canonical_statement: A positive KOH preparation alone is considered sufficient to initiate treatment; if KOH is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, additional confirmatory testing may be performed.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Diagnosis by KOH preparation alone is sufficient for treatment initiation. However, if KOH results are negative and there is high clinical suspicion

canonical_statement: The review generally recommends diagnostic testing before treatment but allows consideration of empiric terbinafine when testing is cost prohibitive.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Diagnostic testing is generally recommended before initiating treatment, but empiric treatment with terbinafine can be considered if testing is cost prohibitive.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Sensitivity 55.9% to 80% (80% used for LR); specificity 95%; LR+ 9.6; LR- 0.4; PV+ 96.3%; PV- 55.9%.

canonical_statement: Treatment selection should use shared decision-making that considers disease severity, treatment duration, cost, comorbidities, interactions, adverse effects, and patient preference.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Shared decision-making based on disease severity, length of treatment, cost, comorbidities, risk of drug-drug interactions, adverse effects, and patient preference

canonical_statement: Oral antifungal therapy is described as the most effective treatment for onychomycosis of any severity and generally has higher cure rates and shorter treatment periods than topical therapy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Oral therapy is the most effective treatment for onychomycosis of any severity.

canonical_statement: Terbinafine is recommended as first-line oral therapy because the review considers it the most effective oral agent for clinical and mycologic cure.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Terbinafine is the most effective oral agent based on its high clinical cure rate

canonical_statement: Chronic or active liver disease is the main contraindication to terbinafine; the review states that baseline transaminases are recommended and subsequent laboratory monitoring is unnecessary in immunocompetent patients.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommends transaminase testing before initiating terbinafine therapy.

canonical_statement: The review identifies tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, tamoxifen, atypical antipsychotics, and beta blockers as drugs that may interact with terbinafine.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Drugs that may interact with concomitant terbinafine therapy include tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, tamoxifen, atypical antipsychotics, and beta blockers.

canonical_statement: The review describes FDA-approved itraconazole regimens as continuous therapy for toenail onychomycosis and pulse dosing for fingernail onychomycosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Continuous itraconazole (Sporanox) therapy is FDA approved for toenail onychomycosis, and a pulse-dosing regimen is approved for fingernail onychomycosis.

canonical_statement: In a five-year prospective study of 144 patients with severe disease summarized by the review, mycologic relapse was higher with itraconazole than terbinafine (53% vs 23%; P < .001).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: mycologic relapse rates are significantly higher with itraconazole than with terbinafine (53% vs. 23%, respectively; P < .001).

population.label: Patients with severe onychomycosis in a five-year prospective study

canonical_statement: In a five-year prospective study of 144 patients with severe disease summarized by the review, clinical relapse was higher with itraconazole than terbinafine (48% vs 21%; P < .001).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: clinical relapse rates are significantly higher with itraconazole than with terbinafine (48% vs. 21%, respectively; P < .001).

population.label: Patients with severe onychomycosis in a five-year prospective study

canonical_statement: The review summarizes a systematic review/network meta-analysis of 22 trials (n=4,205) concluding that terbinafine was likely more effective than itraconazole for complete cure of toenail onychomycosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 22 trials (n = 4,205) ... showed that terbinafine is likely more effective than itraconazole

population.label: Participants in 22 trials of oral antifungal therapy for toenail onychomycosis

canonical_statement: Fluconazole 150 mg weekly for at least six months is described as an off-label alternative when terbinafine or itraconazole cannot be tolerated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Fluconazole (Diflucan), 150 mg weekly for at least six months for fingernails and toenails, may be used as an off-label alternative treatment

canonical_statement: Griseofulvin is rarely used because of longer treatment duration, more adverse events, and lower cure rates than other medications.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Griseofulvin is rarely used because of long treatment duration, higher risk of adverse events, and lower cure rates compared with other medications.

canonical_statement: A systematic review summarized by the article found no significant differences in effectiveness or safety between continuous and pulse-dosing oral antifungal regimens for toenail onychomycosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A systematic review comparing continuous or pulse-dosing oral antifungal regimens ... found no significant differences in effectiveness and safety.

canonical_statement: No systemic therapies were FDA-approved for pediatric onychomycosis in this 2021 review; terbinafine and itraconazole were described as off-label options.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: There are no systemic therapies approved by the FDA for the treatment of onychomycosis in children, although terbinafine and itraconazole are considered off-label treatments.

canonical_statement: For children, topical therapy can be used when three or fewer nails are involved, less than 50% of the nail plate is affected without matrix involvement, or oral therapy is contraindicated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Topical therapy can be used in children if there are three or fewer nails involved, less than 50% of the nail plate surface area is affected with no matrix involvement

canonical_statement: Patients should be counseled that complete nail regrowth usually takes three to six months for fingernails and up to 18 months for toenails.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: fingernails typically take three to six months to completely regrow and toenails can take up to 18 months.

canonical_statement: Topical therapy is less effective and more expensive than oral therapy but may be used as an alternative first-line option for superficial or early distal lateral subungual onychomycosis because adverse effects and interactions are limited.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Although topical therapy is less effective and more expensive than oral therapy, it can be used as an alternative first-line treatment

canonical_statement: The recommended topical treatment duration in the review is 24 weeks for fingernails and 48 weeks for toenails.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The recommended duration of topical therapy is 24 weeks for fingernails and 48 weeks for toenails.

canonical_statement: Topical antifungal adverse effects are generally local and include exfoliation, erythema, burning, and application-site dermatitis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Adverse effects are generally limited to exfoliation, erythema, burning, and dermatitis at the application site.

canonical_statement: In ciclopirox 8% vehicle-controlled RCT study 1 summarized by the review, complete cure at 48 weeks was 5.5% with ciclopirox versus 0.9% with vehicle (P = .059).
In ciclopirox 8% vehicle-controlled RCT study 2 summarized by the review, complete cure at 48 weeks was 8.5% with ciclopirox versus 0% with vehicle (P = .001).
In phase 3 efinaconazole 10% study 1 summarized by the review, complete cure was 17.8% with efinaconazole versus 3.3% with vehicle (P < .001; NNT 7).
In phase 3 efinaconazole 10% study 2 summarized by the review, complete cure was 15.2% with efinaconazole versus 5.5% with vehicle (P < .001; NNT 10).
In phase 3 tavaborole 5% study 1 summarized by the review, complete cure was 6.5% with tavaborole versus 0.5% with vehicle (P < .001; NNT 17).
In phase 3 tavaborole 5% study 2 summarized by the review, complete cure was 9.1% with tavaborole versus 1.5% with vehicle (P < .001; NNT 13).
A small RCT of 24 patients summarized by the review reported an 8% mycologic cure rate with once-weekly amorolfine 5% lacquer for nine months.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A small RCT with 24 patients showed a mycologic cure rate of 8% ... with once-weekly treatment for nine months.

population.label: Participants in a small amorolfine RCT

quantitative_result.original_result_text: 8% mycologic cure rate; once weekly for nine months

canonical_statement: Nail trimming and debridement can be added to oral or topical pharmacologic therapy to increase treatment effectiveness; surgical or nonsurgical nail removal may be considered for severe infection or failed medical therapy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Nail trimming and debridement can be used with oral or topical pharmacologic therapy to increase treatment effectiveness.

canonical_statement: Dual-wavelength infrared and fractional carbon-dioxide laser therapy are described as FDA-approved for temporary cosmetic nail improvement, based on low-level evidence and small RCTs.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dual-wavelength infrared and fractional carbon-dioxide laser therapy are FDA approved for temporary cosmetic improvement of nails based on low-level evidence and small RCTs.

canonical_statement: The review states that combining laser therapy with topical therapy increases overall treatment effectiveness.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Combining laser therapy with topical therapy increases overall treatment effectiveness.

canonical_statement: Small-scale studies of tea tree oil, oregano, vitamin E, bitter orange oil, vinegar soaks, and menthol-camphor ointment are considered insufficient; the review calls for more robust studies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: More robust studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of these essential oils against onychomycosis.

canonical_statement: An uncontrolled plasma-therapy pilot study of 19 participants summarized by the review reported an overall clinical cure rate of 53.8%.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A pilot study of 19 participants without a control group showed an overall clinical cure rate of 53.8%.

population.label: Participants in an uncontrolled plasma-therapy pilot study

quantitative_result.original_result_text: 19 participants without a control group; clinical cure rate 53.8%

canonical_statement: In an unblinded double-dummy RCT of 80 participants summarized by the review, response at 24 weeks was 90% with biweekly photodynamic therapy versus 40% with weekly fluconazole 300 mg (P=.002; NNT 2).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: response to treatment at 24 weeks was greater with photodynamic therapy (90% vs. 40%; P = .002; NNT = 2), this was not a blinded study.

population.label: Participants with confirmed fungal toenail onychomycosis in the photodynamic therapy RCT

canonical_statement: The review concludes that larger randomized trials are needed before photodynamic and plasma therapies can be judged effective and feasible for clinical use.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: larger randomized trials are needed to determine their effectiveness and feasibility for use in the clinical setting.

canonical_statement: The review reports a 20% to 25% relapse rate after successful treatment, with recurrence likely within two years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The relapse rate of onychomycosis is 20% to 25%, with the condition likely to recur within two years of successful therapy.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: relapse rate 20% to 25%; likely within two years

canonical_statement: Poor prognostic features identified in the review include age older than 70 years, prior nail trauma, and diabetes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Features associated with poor prognosis include age older than 70 years, history of nail trauma, and diabetes.

canonical_statement: Based on expert opinion, recurrence prevention includes avoiding barefoot walking in public places, disinfecting shoes and socks, keeping feet cool and dry, and recognizing early recurrence or reinfection.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Based on expert opinion, avoiding walking barefoot in public places may help prevent recurrence.

canonical_statement: The review recommends prompt treatment of tinea pedis because infected skin can serve as a reservoir for recurrent onychomycosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Immediate treatment of tinea pedis can also delay onychomycosis recurrence because the infected skin can act as a reservoir of infection.

canonical_statement: Compared with no prophylaxis, twice-weekly topical antifungal prophylaxis after terbinafine cure was reported to reduce recurrence from 76% to 33% (P<.001).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: twice-weekly prophylaxis with a topical antifungal following terbinafine treatment has been shown to decrease the rate of recurrence (33% vs. 76%; P < .001).

canonical_statement: SORT key recommendation: confirmatory KOH preparation with direct microscopy is recommended before initiating onychomycosis treatment (evidence rating C).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Confirmatory testing using potassium hydroxide preparation with direct microscopy is recommended before initiating treatment for onychomycosis.

canonical_statement: SORT key recommendation: terbinafine has the highest effectiveness and should be first-line therapy for most patients without contraindications (evidence rating B).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Terbinafine has the highest effectiveness of any available therapy and should be recommended as first-line therapy for most patients without contraindications.

canonical_statement: SORT key recommendation: topical therapy can be used for superficial onychomycosis or early distal lateral subungual onychomycosis (evidence rating B).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Topical therapy can be used to treat patients with superficial onychomycosis or early distal lateral subungual onychomycosis.
